summary: Brandon Waselnuk introduces the problem of babysitting agents: when spawned, an agent is a brilliant engineer with zero organizational context. Historically the human was the context engine; now humans are still acting as context engines for their agents. He describes an adoption ladder culminating in a curated context layer (static files like Claude.md) and ultimately a full context engine. Static context files require manual maintenance and lack runtime data, so they are insufficient. A context engine must at runtime pull from the entire corporate knowledge corpus—SaaS apps, systems of record, codebases, Slack, PRs—and reason across all surfaces exhaustively before sending a token-optimized response to the agent. Brandon cites Karpathy: the gap is not intelligence, it is context. He dismantles three myths: naive RAG fails due to satisfaction of search (a radiology phenomenon where the searcher stops at the first finding); MCPs are pipes providing access not understanding; and million-token context windows cannot be reasoned over effectively. He then names six differentiators of a context engine: unified system context, targeted retrieval, conflict resolution, data governance/secure access, personalized relevance via social graphs, and token optimization. He shares hard lessons: optimizing for access alone does not work, unresolved conflicts cause agents to pick arbitrarily, and caching correct answers backfires because stale answers become lies when the system changes. Background agents especially need a context engine to run headlessly without waking humans to ask permission. AI-forward teams deploy context engines across use cases including ask-engineering Slack channels, ticket enrichment, triage, incident management, and coding agents, with teams customizing via a cookbook of skills and standard operating procedures. The recommended workflow uses the engine for planning, runs execution, then leverages the engine again for code review. Brandon demos a social graph tool that builds expert graphs from code repos—showing who works with whom, who reviews what, and which code areas each engineer owns—and announces it will be open-sourced. A second demo shows an MCP-driven query for a Zendesk integration where the agent constructs a research query, triggers explore agents on the right code areas, and produces a correct plan that captures factory patterns and provider registration. His closing vision: an agent should write code that feels like it was written by someone who has been on your team for years.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: The gap in AI agents is context, not intelligence—agents fail because they lack organizational understanding, not reasoning ability.
Access is not understanding: MCPs provide pipes to data but do not reason across surfaces or tell the agent what matters.
Naive RAG fails due to satisfaction of search—agents stop at the first result found and miss the correct approach.
A context engine must deliver six capabilities: unified system context, targeted retrieval, conflict resolution, data governance, personalized relevance via social graphs, and token optimization.
Caching correct answers backfires because systems change—stale cached answers become lies when the codebase evolves.
Background agents need a context engine to run headlessly without waking humans to ask permission questions.

sections.title: Introduction and Framing
sections.summary: Brandon introduces himself and Unblocked, frames the goal of not babysitting agents, and previews three myths and three lessons. He describes agents as brilliant engineers spawned with zero context who need care and feeding.

sections.title: The Context Problem and Adoption Ladder
sections.summary: Brandon traces how humans historically built context at companies and notes that humans are now the context engine for agents. He describes an adoption ladder from fancy autocomplete through agentic IDEs to a curated context layer and ultimately a full context engine.

sections.title: Context Engine Requirements
sections.summary: Explains that static context files are insufficient because they need maintenance and lack runtime data. A context engine must pull from the entire corporate knowledge corpus at runtime, reason across all surfaces exhaustively, and send a token-optimized response to the agent.

sections.title: Three Myths About Building Context
sections.summary: Cites Karpathy that the gap is context not intelligence. Dismantles three myths: naive RAG fails due to satisfaction of search; MCPs are pipes not understanding; million-token context windows cannot be reasoned over effectively. Shows that naive MCP-only run compiled but produced system-breaking code.

sections.title: Context Engine Capabilities
sections.summary: Outlines what a context engine must do: use a social graph as pivot point for personalization, resolve conflicts across sources, respect permissions and data governance through OAuth over MCP, and deliver the right context to the right model at the right time in a token-optimized way.

sections.title: Architecture Overview
sections.summary: Briefly describes Unblocked's architecture: ingesting data sources, processing through six key differentiators, and exposing multiple surface areas where agents and humans interact, including engineers chatting with it in Slack.

sections.title: Six Differentiators and Comparison Results
sections.summary: Names the six differentiators explicitly: unified system context, targeted retrieval, conflict resolution, data governance, personalized relevance via social graphs, and token optimization. Background agents need a context engine to run headlessly. Shows the naive vs. context engine comparison: the naive run missed Bedrock fallback, shipped bugs, and broke custom callers, while the engine run earned a nitpick and merge approval.

sections.title: Hard Lessons Learned
sections.summary: Shares three hard lessons: optimizing for access alone does not work and agents do not self-correct; unresolved conflicts cause agents to pick arbitrarily so conflict resolution is essential; and caching correct answers backfires because systems change, making cached answers stale and misleading. References Anthropic's launch and Ryan's talk confirming context must go into the harness.

sections.title: Use Cases and Customization
sections.summary: Describes how AI-forward teams deploy context engines across ask-engineering Slack channels, ticket enrichment, triage, incident management, and coding. Teams customize via a cookbook of skills, standard operating procedures, workflows, and custom agents. Closing vision: an agent should write code that feels like it was written by someone on your team for years.

sections.title: Demos: Social Graph and MCP Workflow
sections.summary: Demos a social graph tool that builds expert graphs from code repos—showing nodes, edges, who works with whom, who reviews what, and code area ownership—to be open-sourced. A second demo shows an MCP-driven Zendesk integration query where the agent constructs a research query, triggers explore agents on the right code areas, and produces a plan capturing factory patterns and provider registration. Recommends using the engine for planning and code review with execution in between.
